transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-04-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Sana Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Marigold - Head of ML), Priya Nair (Marigold - Eng Manager), Ethan Wu (Marigold - Security)

Summary (auto): Quick intro, baseline traffic and budget, unit cost comp, technical knobs (batch size, cache TTL), deployment options, security needs, agree next steps.

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everybody, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. Sana's our systems engineer, she'll do the deep stuff. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Jordan: Good, thanks. We got a few minutes so we'll jump in. Trying to keep this focused on the economics side.
[00:15] Priya: Yeah, we're specifically trying to understand per request economics and how batching/caching affects our unit cost. We run about 120 reqs/sec at peak, typical prompts are 600-1200 tokens. Budget is...well we can't go over roughly $40k/month for inference if possible.
[00:32] Sana (SE): Cool, that helps. A few clarifying q's — are those tokens input-only, or do you include generated tokens in your billing expectations?
[00:39] Jordan: Right now that's input + output. Our gen is usually 200-600 tokens per response.
[00:45] Alex: To ground this, Redwood hosted per-token list pricing for the models you've seen in the catalog is X per input token and Y per output token — we can share the exact sheet after — but important levers are batch size, prefix cache hit rate, quantized model choices, and whether you run on dedicated reserved capacity.
[01:05] Jordan: Can you give a rough delta between hosted and dedicated? Ballpark.
[01:09] Sana: Sure. Ballpark, hosted list price is higher per-token because we manage the infra and multi-tenant ops. Dedicated reserved capacity comes in with committed monthly pricing — you get lower per-token effective costs because you amortize GPU uptime. For steady throughput like 120 rps, dedicated often wins on cost per-token but requires a commit.
[01:28] Priya: What's the knee for dedicated to make sense? Our usage spikes a lot — some days 2x baseline.
[01:34] Sana: We do burst options for dedicated pools, but typically if you have sustained >80-100 rps with predictable hours, dedicated can be cost-effective. We'll model your traffic curve in the calc.
[01:47] Ethan (Security): Quick sec — we need to confirm data plane isolation if we go dedicated or private. Also K M S integration and audit logs for token level retention.
[01:56] Alex: Totally. For dedicated you get isolated GPU pools and optional VPC peering; for Private we can do on-prem or customer VPC with customer-managed KMS. We'll include our SOC2/ISO artifacts in the security follow-up.
[02:10] Jordan: Back to cost — how much does batching help? Our prompts have a lot of shared prefixes (lots of similar system messages, user meta). We were hearing something about KV prefix caching.
[02:21] Sana: Yes. Two big wins: batching across concurrent requests increases hardware utilization so per-token latency can improve and cost per token falls because the GPU is doing more parallel work. Second, KV cache/prefix caching reduces repeated compute for the same prefix — if you have high cache hit rate for system prompts or common prefix tokens, you can cut the per-response compute significantly. Typical gains vary — we often see 20-60% effective token cost reduction if caching and batching are tuned to the workload.
[02:50] Jordan: 20-60% is a wide band. What determines which side we land on?
[02:54] Sana: Hit rate, sequence length variance, and whether you can tolerate slight added latency from batching. If you accept larger microbatch windows (say 20-50ms additional tail latency) you'll get better batching. Also longer sequences decrease the relative overhead of KV cache, but if you have repeated few-token prompts cache helps more.
[03:15] Priya: Our SLO is 150ms p95 for conversational flows. Would batching push us above that?
[03:21] Sana: We can tune for that. Continuous batching with adaptive windows can keep p95 in range for many workloads. We'll need to run microbenchmarks with your prompt set to pick the configuration that meets p95 while minimizing cost.
[03:35] Jordan: Can we see a worked example? Suppose 1k request/day at 800 tokens in, 400 out, caching hit 30%, what's the per-response cost hosted vs dedicated?
[03:47] Alex: I'll put a simple example in the sheet. Ballpark: hosted might be $0.015 per request under those numbers, dedicated could drop to $0.006-0.01 depending on commit and batch parameters. But that is very workload specific.
[04:06] Priya: That delta matters. Our CFO will ask about amortized GPU cost — do you share the math or just the effective per-token?
[04:13] Alex: We'll share the math: GPU hourly cost, utilization assumptions, effective tokens/sec, cache hit impacts, and an amortized per-token. We'll also show sensitivity to TTL and batch windows.
[04:24] Ethan: On encryption — you mentioned K M S earlier. For private deployment, can we bring our own key? HSM?
[04:31] Sana: Yes, BYOK supported with both cloud KMS and HSM integrations for Private. For Dedicated there's a managed KMS integration; for Private you can bring your own HSM in on-prem scenarios.
[04:40] Jordan: A question on model variants — if we select a quantized variant to save cost, is there a quality hit we should expect? We use specialized medical language; hallucination tolerance is low.
[04:50] Sana: Quantization can slightly impact output distribution; for many workloads differences are minimal, but for sensitive medical nomenclature we recommend running evals on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can produce quality regression alerts and recommend when to avoid quantization for certain flows.
[05:05] Priya: Let's talk scaling — during peak, we spike to 240 rps for 30 minutes. We can't afford cold starts affecting UX.
[05:13] Sana: Dedicated pools with configured autoscaling and burst capacity can handle that. For hosted we have warm pools but at large scale dedicated is more predictable. We can model burst windows and show probability of queueing under different configs.
[05:28] Jordan: Competitor question — if we went with Anthropic or OpenAI, what's different on the cost side?
[05:33] Alex: Anthropic/OpenAI pricing differs; many of those providers charge per-token too but with different rate cards and fewer dedicated/private options out of the box. We can provide a competitor comp in the deck; but main difference is Redwood's routing and batch optimizations plus dedicated/private deployment options.
[05:50] Priya: Can you elaborate on routing? We have sensitive flows vs non-sensitive; we may want certain requests to go private while others go hosted to save cost.
[05:58] Sana: That's supported — policy-based routing lets you route by label, token size, customer tier. You can set fallback to hosted if private capacity is saturated. That hybrid approach often yields best cost/perf balance.
[06:10] Jordan: Regarding retention and logs — we want to avoid storing PHI. Can we disable logging for some routes?
[06:17] Alex: Yes, route-level log controls and token redaction options exist. We'll include the specifics in the security packet.
[06:25] Ethan: Also need to know audit log granularity — do you provide token-level audit trails or just request-level metadata?
[06:31] Sana: We provide request-level metadata by default and optional more granular logs; in Private deployments you can control retention and export into your SIEM.

[06:45] Jordan: So next question is the pilot scope — we want to pilot a tiny production path for the triage assistant with realistic load — maybe 2-4 instances, run for 30 days. We want to hit p95 150ms and keep costs under $8k for the month.
[06:58] Alex: That sounds doable to scope. We'll propose a pilot plan with an SLO and budget cap and agree on measurement.
[07:06] Priya: For the pilot, would you recommend hosted first or dedicated?
[07:10] Sana: For short 30-day pilots, hosted is faster to start and lower upfront. If you want commit-level savings from day one, dedicated can be done but needs contracts. I'd recommend hosted + reserved burst settings for initial pilot and then move to Dedicated for ramp.
[07:25] Jordan: What about cold-starts in hosted? We can't have first-request latency spikes.
[07:30] Alex: We can configure warm pools and health probes; we also provide pre-warm options for critical instances — extra cost but predictable latency.

[07:40] Jordan: Can we get a worked example with Marigold's actual prompt set? Like real numbers.
[07:44] Sana: Yes — Sana: we'll need the sample prompts and a small dataset, plus a call to confirm privacy level. We'll run a microbench and return latency/cost curves.
[07:54] Alex: We'll also include a sensitivity chart: x-axis = cache hit rate; lines for different batch windows; y-axis = effective cost per request. That will make the decision clear for CFO.

[Timestamps jump — mid-call deeper technical dive]
[15:02] Sana: Quick note on KV cache: it's not a simple LRU — we maintain context-keyed caches with TTL and consistency rules; cache misses still involve full attention compute. For medical abbreviations cache hit accuracy matters — mismatches can cause slight tokenization diffs.
[15:26] Jordan: Sounds technical — the TL;DR is we need to know cache hit probability for our flows.
[15:31] Sana: Right. We'll instrument the pilot to report cache-hit rates and per-token compute saved.

[22:10] Priya: If batching increases p95 by 30ms but reduces cost by 40%, the tradeoff seems fine. We need to model it though.
[22:18] Sana: Exactly. That's why microbenchmarks with your real traffic shape are necessary.

[33:45] Ethan: Security team will want SAML SSO for access, RBAC roles, and dedicated audit streams. Also contractual language around data deletion.
[33:54] Alex: We'll loop in our security team; we have standard SAML integrations and can map roles. We'll also provide DPA clauses and deletion commitment language.

[44:03] Jordan: A practical ask: can you provide an 'upper bound' cost if caching is zero and there's no batching? Our execs ask for worst-case scenarios.
[44:12] Alex: Yes. We'll include worst-case (no cache, minimal batching) and best-case (high cache, aggressive batching) numbers in the model. Worst-case is simply list price tokens multiplied by expected tokens; we'll show both.

[51:20] Priya: Any gotchas about multi-tenant hosted that we should watch for? e.g., noisy neighbor problems.
[51:27] Sana: For hosted, we have strict isolation in software and autoscaling safeguards; noisy neighbor can appear at microsecond tail latencies but rarely affects p95 unless you have very large peaks. Dedicated avoids this by giving you reserved GPU capacity.

[56:00] Alex (AE) Recap: Okay quick recap — action items: we'll share the detailed cost model and competitor comp, Sana will run benchmark on your prompt corpus, Marigold will send sample prompts and compliance list, and we'll schedule security follow-up. Expected deliveries: cost sheet by 2025-04-10, micro-benchmark results by 2025-04-11, security packet meeting week of 2025-04-14.
[56:30] Jordan: Sounds good. Priya/Ethan anything else?
[56:36] Priya: No, good. Thanks.
[56:38] Ethan: Thanks all.
[56:40] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites. Bye.

Auto-generated Action items: Alex — share cost model; Sana — run micro-bench; Marigold — send prompts & compliance list.
